The Elbe River. A seven hundred and twenty-four mile river flowing from the Czech Republic through eastern Germany to the North Sea, passing through major cities like Dresden and Hamburg. It has been central to German and Baltic trade, and the Elbe valley's beauty inspired Romantic-era painters and poets.

The Elbe originates in the Czech Riesengebirge mountains and flows northwest through Saxony, Bohemia, and Hamburg before emptying into the North Sea. Hamburg, situated at the Elbe's mouth, became one of Europe's major ports. The Hanseatic League's power partly depended on Elbe commerce. The Saxon Switzerland region along the Elbe near Dresden features dramatic sandstone cliffs and gorges that inspired Romantic landscape painters.

The river served as a natural border dividing Cold War Germany. The Elbe was famously the meeting point of American and Soviet forces in nineteen forty-five. However, the river has been heavily industrialized. Pollution from lignite mining and industrial sites in East Germany left a lasting legacy that extended well into the post-Cold War era. The Elbe valley near Meissen is famous for porcelain production. Meissen's position on the river enabled trade in this luxury good across Europe.

The Elbe flows through the heart of German territory and shaped its geography fundamentally. It was also a shared resource between Germany and the Czech Republic. Hamburg, one of Europe's greatest ports, is built at the Elbe's mouth. The river was a crucial trade route for northern European medieval commerce under the Hanseatic League, connecting distant lands through commerce and culture.
